title: Lesson 38: Governor-Limit-Aware Design: SOQL, SOSL, and DML Budgets
description: The arithmetic behind limit exceptions: how SOQL statements, query rows, DML statements, and DML rows are metered, and why the statement and row meters fail at completely different batch sizes.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Governor-Limit-Aware Design: SOQL, SOSL, and DML Budgets”, a loop updates one record per iteration and fails at the 151st record. Which meter fired, and what does the other meter show?
options: The DML row meter at 10,000 rows, with the statement meter already at its ceiling.
The DML statement meter at 150, while the row meter has barely moved, because one update on a collected list costs a single statement.
The SOQL statement meter at 100, because every update implies a query.
The query row meter at 50,000 rows, which no amount of batching can change.
questions.explanation: Statement count and row count are independent counters, and batching the same work into one DML call buys statement headroom, which is the scarce resource in a synchronous save.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson’s guidance?
options: 50,000 rows is the DML row ceiling, and it resets with each batch execute chunk.
Scheduled Apex gets the higher asynchronous budget: 200 queries, 12 MB of heap, and 60,000 milliseconds of CPU.
Moving to async roughly doubles the query and CPU budget and does nothing for DML, so a transaction failing on DML rows will not be saved by async alone.
A parent-child subquery inside a SOQL query is free, because it is part of a single top-level statement.
questions.explanation: Async raises query count, heap, and CPU, while DML stays at 150 statements and 10,000 rows and SOQL stays at 50,000 rows, so the meter that is failing decides whether async helps at all.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: The query and DML budget belongs to the transaction rather than to your code, so a design review asks who else touches this object in the same save and deliberately leaves headroom.
Certified managed packages share the org’s pool, which is why installing one can halve the available queries.
The 50 million row figure applies to any Database.getQueryLocator call, including one inside a synchronous transaction.
System.runAs is a test-only construct and does not consume DML statements.
questions.explanation: Everything firing on the save spends from one pool, so headroom and a budget sheet listing every consumer, including uncertified packages, are what keep a limit exception out of production.
